title: Keel's limits are deliberately asymmetric: risk-increasing operations are capped while unwinding is unlimited
content:
Reading the Ethereum limits as pairs makes the pattern unmistakable. `LIMIT_USDS_MINT` is "`maxAmount`: 10,000 USDS, `slope`: 10,000 USDS per day" while `LIMIT_USDS_BURN` is "`maxAmount`: Unlimited, `slope`: Unlimited" (A.6.1.1.3.2.6.1.2.1.1.3.1.1.1–2). `LIMIT_4626_DEPOSIT` into sUSDS is 100,000,000 with a 50,000,000/day slope, while `LIMIT_4626_WITHDRAW` is "`maxAmount`: Unlimited, `slope`: 0" (…3.1.2.1–2).

The rule being expressed is that a rate limit exists to bound *exposure*, and an operation that reduces exposure needs no bound. Burning USDS retires liability; withdrawing from a vault returns capital to the controller. Throttling either would be actively harmful in the emergency the limits are designed for — a system that rate-limits its own exit is one that cannot deleverage during a crisis.

A subtlety worth catching: withdrawal is Unlimited with a slope of 0. A zero slope is coherent only because the maximum is already unbounded, so there is no budget to refill — the unlimited case is expressed by disabling the mechanism rather than by a large number.

The mint limit is the other tell. At 10,000 USDS against swap and bridge limits of 100 million, Keel is effectively not authorized to create USDS at scale inside the Liquidity Layer; it is authorized to move and convert USDS that already exists. Issuance capacity stays with Sky, and the Allocator Vault's own parameters are defined upstream at A.3.7.1.2.1.4 rather than in Keel's Artifact.
description: USDS burn and sUSDS withdrawal carry maxAmount 'Unlimited' while minting is capped at 10,000 USDS and deposits at 100M — the system never throttles a retreat to safety.
